shortlist.name: Paul Godines
shortlist.headline: Automation Engineer | Building Tested, Trusted & Trained Maintenance, Operations & Automation Engineering Teams Using Interactive Simulation Training
shortlist.why_now: Commented on Alicia Lomas's post about software standing in for missing mechanical protection. His line — 'Should this problem be solved in code at all?' — is the exact frame Chris uses when plants ask for IIoT monitoring on mechanically compromised equipment. He builds simulation training for automation/maintenance teams, which is directly adjacent to IIoT adoption bottlenecks.
shortlist.signal: This is such a classic controls war story. Software can monitor, alarm, trend, interlock, and shut things down, but it should not be the only thing standing between a bad mechanical design and self-destruction.
shortlist.opener: Your comment on Alicia's post landed on the right question. We hit a version of it constantly on the IIoT side: plants asking for monitoring data from machines that have underlying mechanical problems, and having to be clear about what a current-signature alarm can catch versus what it cannot replace. The simulation training work you are doing is interesting to me — the bottleneck on IIoT rollouts in our experience is rarely the hardware or protocol; it is the maintenance and ops teams knowing what to do with the signal. Curious whether you are seeing that same gap from your side.

shortlist.name: Abhisek Chakrabarti
shortlist.headline: Smart Operations, Intelligent Assets & Scalable Digital Ecosystems | Smart Plant, AI, IIoT & ESG | Delivering £100M+ ROI in Manufacturing | Views My Own
shortlist.why_now: Engaged on David Schultz's knowledge-graph post with a specific number: 20-30% of data value lost on industrial deployments that lack ISA-95 ontology anchor. Shows he has real deployment experience, not just advisory framing. IIoT + Smart Plant + manufacturing ROI is a direct match.
shortlist.signal: The real issue isn't graph vs database — it's semantic alignment. In many industrial deployments, 20-30% of data value is lost because models aren't anchored to shared ontologies like ISA-95.
shortlist.opener: Your ISA-95 anchor point on David Schultz's post matches what we see on brownfield deployments. The standard gets agreed in the architecture phase and then the MQTT topic trees end up bespoke anyway because the SI adapted to the existing PLC naming scheme. We build edge hardware that publishes SparkplugB, so the naming discipline conversation is practical for us on every installation. Happy to compare notes on where that breakdown actually happens — the 20-30% number you cited is consistent with what we observe.

shortlist.name: Wenhui Zhang, PhD
shortlist.headline: Shaping Industrial AI & Digital Manufacturing Platform | Guiding System Architecture from Shopfloor to Data & AI | Germany-China Industry Experience
shortlist.why_now: Made the ISA-95 connection explicit on Schultz's post and asked a precise technical question about knowledge vs. data graph distinction. 'Shopfloor to Data & AI' architecture is exactly Chris's stack direction. Germany-China manufacturing background suggests real brownfield exposure.
shortlist.signal: If I understand correctly, you refer data graph to data with bespoke naming conventions and bespoke relationships, and knowledge graph to standard data model such as ISA-95.
shortlist.opener: Your ISA-95 framing on David's post is the right lens. The gap between a data graph and a knowledge graph shows up clearly at the edge layer: you can publish every machine signal over MQTT with a disciplined SparkplugB schema and still end up with a data graph if the asset model is not shared upstream. We see it on brownfield installs where the PLC naming predates any standard. Your work on shopfloor-to-AI architecture sits in that same territory — curious what you are finding as the hardest layer to get right.

shortlist.name: Bastien Carel
shortlist.headline: Smart Manufacturing & Digital Transformation | IIoT · MES · Digital Twin | 20 Years Bridging Operations & Technology | CM2(C) | Bias for Action
shortlist.why_now: 20 years bridging operations and technology, explicitly IIoT + MES. The MES integration layer is where most of Chris's customers are right now: machine data flowing, but connecting it to production order context is the next step. Engaging on the Schultz knowledge-graph post signals he is thinking about data modeling, not just connectivity.
shortlist.signal: Great analogy with the family tree. (on Schultz's knowledge graph post)
shortlist.opener: Your background bridging operations and IIoT over 20 years maps closely to what we work on. We build edge hardware for signal-level machine connectivity on brownfield equipment, publishing over MQTT and SparkplugB. The MES integration question is where most of our customers are right now: machine data is flowing, but connecting it to the production order context is the step that unlocks scheduling and OEE. Curious whether you are seeing a consistent pattern for how plants approach that connection, or whether it is bespoke every time.

shortlist.name: Michele Brami
shortlist.headline: Autopiloting the boring work. System Integrator & Architect
shortlist.why_now: Specifically mentioned writing a series on ontologies and ISA-95 modeled UNS (Unified Namespace). That is directly Chris's territory: SparkplugB, MQTT topic discipline, brownfield asset modeling. An SI who is writing publicly about UNS is worth talking to.
shortlist.signal: It's incredible how much your post is near my upcoming series of articles about ontologies and ISA-95 modeled UNS.
shortlist.opener: Your upcoming series on ISA-95 UNS is timely. Most implementations I see are still bespoke MQTT topic trees rather than a properly anchored Unified Namespace — the discipline tends to get traded away during brownfield deployment when the SI has to adapt to whatever the existing PLC naming scheme is. We publish SparkplugB from edge hardware on brownfield machines, so the topic-model discipline question is practical for us, not theoretical. Would be interested to read your framing on where the ISA-95 model actually helps versus where it becomes a compliance exercise.
